hints: Recall that Young modulus $E$ is measured in $\text{Pa}$ and is defined by $E = \text{stress} / \text{strain}$ for copper wire stretching.
Think about how stiff copper is: a large tensile stress of order $10^{8} \text{Pa}$ produces only a very small strain of order $10^{-3}$.
Combine that stiffness idea to estimate $E$ as a large stress divided by a tiny strain, giving a power of ten far above $10^{4} \text{Pa}$.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the power of ten closest to the Young modulus of copper, with unit $\text{Pa}$.
State the governing relation $E = \sigma / \varepsilon$, where stress $\sigma = F/A$ in $\text{Pa}$ and strain $\varepsilon = \Delta L / L$ has no unit.
Recall that metals are very stiff, so a copper wire needs a stress of order $10^{8} \text{Pa}$ to give a strain of only about $10^{-3}$.
Estimate $E \approx 10^{8} / 10^{-3} = 10^{11} \text{Pa}$, so the order of magnitude is $10^{11} \text{Pa}$.

options.A: A value of $10^{-11} \text{Pa}$ is far too small and would mean copper deforms enormously under tiny stress, which is opposite to a stiff metal.
options.B: A value of $10^{-4} \text{Pa}$ is still extremely soft, more like an almost zero stiffness, not a strong metallic lattice.
options.C: A value of $10^{4} \text{Pa}$ is typical of very soft rubber-like materials, not a metal that needs huge stress for small strain.
options.D: A value of $10^{11} \text{Pa}$ matches copper at about $10^{11} \text{Pa}$, reflecting very large stress needed for unit strain.
